name: Zion Williamson
notes: A 284-lb Duke freshman phenomenon (22.6 ppg on a nation's-second-best 68% FG), a "once-in-a-generation" athlete per Kevin Durant, with unorthodox shot mechanics and questioned defensive effort as the honest concerns beneath the highlight reels. New Orleans took him 1st. Williamson flashed exactly that superstar upside early — All-Rookie honors, a 27.0 ppg season, a 2021 All-Star nod — but a Jones fracture wiped out all of 2021-22, and a chain of hamstring, weight and conditioning issues has limited him to as few as 30 games in some seasons since, though he returned for 62 games at 21.0 ppg in 2025-26. Solid outcome: legitimate superstar-level talent and production whenever healthy, permanently undercut by durability.

name: Ja Morant
notes: An unranked Murray State recruit with only one high-major offer, who became the first player in NCAA history to average 20 points and 10 assists in a season — elite athleticism and vision from a mid-major, size (6'2") the only real question. Memphis took him 2nd. Morant delivered spectacularly on the court — Rookie of the Year, multiple All-Star and All-NBA selections, a Most Improved Player award — but a string of gun-related Instagram incidents brought two suspensions (8 and 25 games) in 2023, and shoulder and elbow injuries limited him to as few as 9-20 games in recent seasons, culminating in a June 2026 trade to Portland after seven years in Memphis. Hit: a true star-level talent whose on-court brilliance was matched by real off-court and durability turbulence.

name: RJ Barrett
notes: A consensus top recruit playing alongside Zion and Reddish at Duke, a "cold-blooded killer" scorer and ball-handler whose free-throw (66.5%) and three-point (30.8%) shooting were flagged as real growth areas. New York took him 3rd. Barrett developed steadily into a genuine scorer (a 46-point game, a $120M extension) before a trade to his hometown Raptors unlocked more well-rounded play — a first career triple-double and a dramatic Game 7-forcing overtime shot in the 2026 playoffs. Solid outcome: a real, franchise-caliber scoring wing, never quite the superstar his recruiting class implied.

name: De'Andre Hunter
notes: Virginia's title-run co-star and NABC Defensive Player of the Year (15.2/5.1, 27 points in the championship game), elite perimeter defense with developing offensive consistency the flag. Was taken 4th (Lakers, immediately dealt through New Orleans to Atlanta). Hunter spent six solid seasons in Atlanta (two 35-point games) before a 2025 trade to Cleveland and a further 2026 trade to Sacramento, where a retinal detachment from an eye injury ended his season early. Mixed outcome: a real, long two-way NBA role, injuries and multiple trades keeping him from a defined long-term home.

name: Darius Garland
notes: Vanderbilt's five-star, top-ranked point guard recruit whose season ended after just five games (a 33-point outburst against Liberty included) due to a meniscus injury — real talent, a thin and injury-shortened sample. Cleveland took him 5th. Garland struggled as a rookie before breaking out fully — multiple All-Star selections, a $231M extension, a 51-point game, and a key role on Cleveland's East-best 2025-26 team — before a February 2026 trade to the Clippers for James Harden. Hit: the elite point-guard talent scouted, delayed by the injury-shortened evaluation, became a genuine All-Star.

name: Jarrett Culver
notes: Texas Tech's Big 12 Player of the Year and national runner-up (18.5/6.4 as a sophomore), real perimeter scoring versatility undercut by a rough shooting night in the title game (5-of-22) that hinted at consistency questions. Phoenix took him 6th (traded to Minnesota). Culver's rookie year (9.2 ppg, real minutes) proved to be the ceiling — his role shrank every year after through Memphis and Atlanta, down to sub-4 ppg by 2021-22. Bust: real college production and athleticism that never became NBA-level shot-making consistency.

name: Coby White
notes: A five-star UNC freshman who passed Michael Jordan on the program's all-time freshman scoring list, elite offensive talent whose modest assist numbers (4.1) raised real point-guard-versus-scorer role questions. Chicago took him 7th. White's first four seasons were inconsistent (9.7-15.1 ppg, unclear role) before a genuine 2023-24 breakout (runner-up Most Improved Player), a 44-point game, and back-to-back Player of the Week awards (a feat last matched by Jordan), before a 2026 trade to Charlotte and a $74M re-signing. Solid outcome: a legitimate late-blooming NBA scoring option after years of inconsistency.

name: Jaxson Hayes
notes: A Texas freshman with elite efficiency (10.0/5.0 on 72.8% FG, 2.2 blocks, Big 12 Freshman of the Year and All-Defensive), pure rim-running/rim-protecting upside from a thin one-and-done sample, plus a late-season knee injury. New Orleans took him 8th. Hayes had real flashes (10.7/5.7 over a late-2022 stretch) before his role shrank, then found a steady reserve role with the Lakers (35 starts in 2024-25) and a 2026 move to Utah. Mixed outcome: a real, sustained NBA rotation big, never the anchor his efficiency once promised.

name: Rui Hachimura
notes: Gonzaga's WCC Player of the Year and consensus All-American as a junior (19.7/6.5, Maui Invitational MVP, a 20-point/5-assist upset of Duke), the fifth Japanese-born Division I player, real scoring versatility with athletic-ceiling questions. Washington took him 9th. Hachimura developed steadily (12-13 ppg over four Wizards seasons, improved to 44.7% from three) before a 2023 trade to the Lakers unlocked a bigger role — a 2023 NBA Cup title, a 36-point game, a contract extension — and a 2026 move to the Clippers. Mixed outcome: a real, valuable NBA scoring forward for years, never quite the go-to option his college peak suggested.

name: Cam Reddish
notes: A five-star Duke recruit playing in Zion and Barrett's shadow (13.5 ppg, only 33% from three, Honorable Mention All-ACC despite elite recruiting rank), real talent but real shot-selection and engagement questions even at Duke. Atlanta took him 10th. Reddish flashed early (10-11 ppg over two seasons, a 36-point game) but never solidified a role, bouncing through New York, Portland and the Lakers within three years and fading to 3.2 ppg by 2024-25 before being waived. Bust: five-star talent that never resolved the consistency and engagement concerns flagged even in college.

name: Cameron Johnson
notes: A UNC senior called "the best shooter in the draft" (16.9/5.8/2.4 on 50.6/45.7% shooting, a 26-point night at Duke), pure shot-making the calling card, positional versatility and defense the open questions. Minnesota took him 11th (traded to Phoenix). Johnson developed into a real 3-and-D wing — a 2021 Finals run, a 38-point outburst, a $94.5M Brooklyn deal with an 18.8 ppg season — before a 2025 trade to Denver (for Michael Porter Jr.) and a knee injury that he returned from by February 2026. Hit: elite college shooting that became a genuine, well-paid NBA scoring wing.

name: P.J. Washington
notes: A five-star Kentucky forward who played through a pinkie injury as a freshman before breaking out as a junior (15.2/7.5 on 52%+ FG, 42.3% from three as a sophomore), real stretch-four skill. Charlotte took him 12th. Washington made the most three-pointers in any NBA debut ever, developed into a steady scorer (peaking at 15.7 ppg), and after a 2024 trade to Dallas helped lead the Mavericks to the 2024 Finals, signing an $88.76M extension. Solid outcome: a genuine, sustained NBA starter and Finals contributor.

name: Tyler Herro
notes: A one-and-done Kentucky freshman (14.0/4.5/2.5) valued purely for shooting touch and scoring versatility, all-around playmaking and defense the clear developmental questions. Miami took him 13th. Herro became the first Heat player to win Sixth Man of the Year (2022), battled injuries before a full breakout — a 2025 All-Star selection and Three-Point Contest title, a 23.9 ppg career-best season — before a stunning July 2026 trade sending him to Milwaukee in exchange for Giannis Antetokounmpo. Hit: a shooting specialist who developed into a genuine All-Star-level scorer.

name: Romeo Langford
notes: Indiana's top-rated shooting guard recruit nationally, the third-highest-scoring freshman in program history (16.5 ppg) despite playing through a torn thumb ligament — real scoring talent with an already-present durability flag. Boston took him 14th. A wrist injury wiped out his entire rookie season, and Langford never developed past marginal minutes (3.5 ppg over three Boston seasons) before a trade to San Antonio and a shift to the G League. Bust: the exact durability concern flagged pre-draft compounded into a career-defining pattern of injury.

name: Sekou Doumbouya
notes: An 18-year-old French forward (Pascal Siakam/Draymond Green athletic comps) with a 6'11" wingspan and real defensive versatility, but genuine questions about polish and shot-making consistency given his youth. Detroit took him 15th, the youngest player in the league that season. Doumbouya flashed real scoring upside early (a 24-point game) but his role shrank every season after, and multiple trades (Brooklyn, Houston — waived within days) sent him to a two-way deal with the Lakers before his career shifted to Spain, winning a 2023 G League title along the way. Bust: elite tools that never became consistent enough NBA production.

name: Chuma Okeke
notes: An Auburn sophomore breakout (12.0/6.8/1.8 stl/1.2 blk) who tore his ACL in the Sweet 16 en route to Auburn's first Final Four, real lottery-caliber talent with the injury the only reason he fell. Orlando took him 16th, ESPN calling him a potential "steal." Salary-cap issues delayed his debut a year, and Okeke's best stretch (8.6/5.0 in 2021-22) never repeated — production collapsed to 2.3 ppg by 2023-24, and he bounced through the Knicks, 76ers and Cavaliers on 10-day deals before signing with Real Madrid in 2025. Bust: real lottery talent that recurring injuries and inconsistent opportunity never let fully develop.

name: Nickeil Alexander-Walker
notes: A Virginia Tech sophomore breakout (16.5/4.1/4.0) who helped a Sweet 16 run, a mid-first-round grade on all-around guard skill rather than a lottery-caliber profile. Brooklyn took him 17th (traded to New Orleans). Alexander-Walker developed gradually (5.7 to 12.8 ppg over three Pelicans seasons), found real rotation stability in Minnesota, then had a full breakout with Atlanta in 2025-26 — the 2026 Most Improved Player award, a 20.8 ppg season (the third-largest scoring jump in 25 years) and a franchise three-point record. Hit: a mid-first-round guard whose late-career breakout validated real star-level upside.

name: Goga Bitadze
notes: A 19-year-old Georgian center (Mega Basket in Serbia) who won EuroLeague Rising Star and ABA League MVP honors, real shot-blocking and rebounding but explicitly raw offense. Indiana took him 18th as a developmental project. Bitadze needed years of limited bench minutes (3.2 to 7.0 ppg over four Pacers seasons) before a 2023 move to Orlando finally unlocked him — a $25M extension and a genuine 2024-25 breakout (7.2/6.6 across 70 games, 42 starts). Solid outcome: a real, patiently-developed NBA rotation center, exactly the long-term project scouted.

name: Luka Šamanić
notes: A Croatian forward (No. 39 on ESPN's Top 100) with real athleticism and defensive upside, one of a record 58 international prospects that draft, still raw against pro-level competition. San Antonio took him 19th. Šamanić never found consistent NBA minutes — 86 total games across four seasons (4.5/2.4), waived by the Spurs and unable to stick on two-way deals with New York, Boston or Utah — before his career shifted to Turkey, Croatia, Spain and, by 2025, Russia. Bust: real athletic upside that never resolved into an NBA-level offensive game.

name: Matisse Thybulle
notes: Washington's Naismith Defensive Player of the Year and Lefty Driesell Award winner — the only player in two decades to record 100+ steals and 80+ blocks in a season — elite defensive instincts with a clear, acknowledged offensive limitation (9.2 ppg, 35.8% from three career). Boston took him 20th (traded to Philadelphia). Thybulle became exactly the elite defensive specialist scouted — two All-Defensive Second Teams despite limited minutes — before a 2023 trade to Portland (a $33M extension), injury-limited 2025-26, and a 2026 move to the Lakers. Mixed outcome: a genuine, sustained elite-defense NBA role player, the offensive limitation never resolving as feared.

name: Brandon Clarke
notes: Gonzaga's first-ever WCC Newcomer and Defensive Player of the Year in the same season, a preternatural finisher and rim protector (a 36-point, 8-rebound, 5-block tournament game putting him alongside Shaq and David Robinson) whose lack of shooting range was the clear NBA question. Oklahoma City took him 21st (traded to Memphis). Clarke delivered immediately — All-Rookie First Team, real playoff production — before a torn Achilles in 2023 and further knee and calf injuries steadily eroded his availability, down to just 2 games in his final season. Solid outcome: real, immediate two-way production at his peak, cut short by injuries; Clarke died in May 2026 at age 29.

name: Grant Williams
notes: Tennessee's two-time consensus All-American and SEC Player of the Year, a physical, high-IQ forward whose translatable NBA skill was defensive versatility and toughness rather than a finished offensive game. Boston took him 22nd. Williams became a real rotation piece and locker-room leader for Boston (part of the 2022 Finals run) before a 2023 sign-and-trade to Dallas and a 2024 trade to Charlotte, developing into a legitimate stretch-four/small-ball-five option. Hit: a defense-and-toughness college star who carved out a genuine, valuable NBA career.

name: Darius Bazley
notes: A five-star, McDonald's All-American who skipped college entirely — first flirting with a G League deal, then taking a $1M New Balance internship instead — an unconventional, largely untested path that even Jim Boeheim publicly doubted. Utah took him 23rd (traded to Oklahoma City). Bazley had one real productive stretch (13.7/7.2 in 2020-21) before a tibial plateau fracture derailed him, and stops in Phoenix, Philadelphia and Utah never recovered that form — a 2026 incident (pushing a teammate) getting him cut by Houston. Bust: elite recruiting pedigree that an unorthodox, undertested pre-draft path never fully validated.

name: Ty Jerome
notes: A Virginia junior and Bob Cousy Award finalist (13.6/5.5) on a No. 1 seed team, secondary-playmaking skill projected as an early-second-round value. Philadelphia took him 24th (traded to Phoenix). Ankle and groin injuries repeatedly slowed him through Phoenix, Oklahoma City, Golden State and Cleveland, but Jerome kept finding real minutes when healthy (10.7 ppg in 2020-21), signing a $28M Memphis deal in 2025 and opening 2026 with a 20-point Grizzlies debut. Hit: a smart, skilled college guard whose NBA value, though injury-interrupted, proved real and lasting.

name: Nassir Little
notes: A consensus top-2 high school recruit nationally whose lone UNC season (9.8/4.6) undersold the hype, real athletic upside but a thin, limited-role sample. Portland took him 25th. Little's third season flashed real promise (9.8 ppg, career-high minutes) before a shoulder labral tear and multiple abdominal surgeries derailed him, production collapsing with Phoenix (3.4 ppg) before a shift to the G League and Japan's B.League by 2025. Bust: elite recruiting pedigree undone by injuries before it could translate to NBA production.

name: Dylan Windler
notes: Belmont's four-year star who broke out dramatically as a senior (21.3/10.8 on 42.9% from three), real shooting and rebounding versatility from a mid-major. Cleveland took him 26th. A stress reaction in his leg cost him his entire rookie season before he ever played, and Windler never recovered momentum — just 101 total NBA games (3.2 ppg) across Cleveland, the Knicks, Lakers and Hawks on marginal deals. Bust: a legitimate senior-year breakout that a pre-rookie injury never let get a fair NBA test.

name: Mfiondu Kabengele
notes: A redshirt Florida State sophomore who broke out as ACC Sixth Man of the Year (13.2/5.9/1.5 blk) and elevated further in the tournament (17.0/8.0/2.0 blk), real scoring punch off the bench. Brooklyn took him 27th (traded to the Clippers). Kabengele never found consistent NBA minutes (3.5 ppg as a rookie declining to 1.2 the next year) across the Clippers, Cavaliers, Rockets and Celtics, his career shifting to Europe by 2023. Bust: real tournament-stage scoring that never scaled to NBA competition.

name: Jordan Poole
notes: A Michigan combo guard valued purely for shooting range and athleticism, with explicitly flagged polish and fundamentals concerns entering the draft. Golden State took him 28th. Poole needed a G League runway before breaking out fully — an NBA-leading free-throw percentage, a key role in the 2022 championship alongside Curry and Thompson — before a 2023 trade to Washington (a franchise-record 235 threes) and a 2025 move to New Orleans, where injuries and inefficiency dropped him to a career-low 13.4 ppg in 2025-26. Mixed outcome: a genuine championship contributor at his Golden State peak, production and efficiency declining meaningfully since.

name: Keldon Johnson
notes: A top-15 Kentucky recruit (13.5/5.9 on 46.1/38.1% shooting) who declared after one season, real perimeter shot-making and glass work from a limited freshman sample. San Antonio took him 29th. Johnson developed into a full-time starter (a 22.0 ppg peak season, an $80M extension) before a role change to Sixth Man of the Year-caliber bench scoring in 2025-26 (13.2/5.4, all 82 games) as the Spurs reached the 2026 Finals. Solid outcome: the longest-tenured Spur, a real, sustained double-digit NBA scorer for his entire career so far.

name: Kevin Porter Jr.
notes: A USC freshman with elite shot-creation and James Harden-style isolation scoring, undercut by real flagged concerns — poor shot selection, a bad assist-to-turnover ratio, weak free-throw shooting, and off-court red flags. Milwaukee took him 30th (traded to Cleveland). A weapons charge and locker-room tension in Cleveland led to a trade to Houston, where Porter became the youngest player ever with a 50-point, 10-assist game — but a 2023 domestic violence arrest derailed his career further, and stints in Greece, the Clippers, Oklahoma City and Milwaukee (17.4/7.4 across 38 games before season-ending knee surgery in 2026) have made his career a persistent story of talent undermined by off-court instability. Mixed outcome: real, occasionally historic offensive production, permanently shadowed by the character concerns flagged pre-draft.

name: Nic Claxton
notes: A three-star Georgia recruit who broke out as a junior (13.0/8.6/2.5 blk on 46% FG), real length and defensive versatility as a developmental center project. Brooklyn took him 31st. Injuries slowed his first two seasons (hamstring, shoulder surgery), but once Brooklyn traded Jarrett Allen, Claxton took over as the primary center — leading the league in field goal percentage (70.5%) in 2022-23, a $100M extension in 2024, and a 2026 trade to Chicago. Hit: a developmental second-round center pick who became a genuine, well-paid starting-caliber defensive anchor.

name: KZ Okpala
notes: A four-star Stanford sophomore breakout (16.9/5.7 on 46.5/37.5% shooting), real size and shooting touch for a wing. Phoenix took him 32nd (traded to Miami). An Achilles strain limited his rookie year to 5 games, and Okpala never recovered momentum — a steadily shrinking role through Miami, Oklahoma City and Sacramento (never topping 3.7 ppg) before falling out of the league by 2023. Bust: real college shooting production that an early injury and thin opportunity never let translate.

name: Carsen Edwards
notes: Purdue's Elite Eight legend, setting an NCAA tournament record with 28 threes across four games (a 10-of-19 outburst against Virginia), elite shot-making volume undercut by a real efficiency dip as a junior (39.4% FG) and a small (5'11") frame. Boston took him 33rd. Edwards never found an NBA role (72 games across three seasons, 3.7 ppg on 36.4% shooting) before his career shifted to Europe, where he's since become a genuine star — a 2025 All-EuroLeague First Team scoring leader. Bust at the NBA level, a real EuroLeague star instead.

name: Bruno Fernando
notes: A physical Maryland sophomore (13.6/10.6/1.9 blk, First-Team All-Big Ten) with real rebounding and rim-protection production, limited range and playmaking the flags. Philadelphia took him 34th (traded to Atlanta). Fernando settled into a well-traveled backup center career — Atlanta, Boston, Houston (a $10.9M deal), back to Atlanta, then Toronto — never exceeding modest reserve production (4.0 ppg career) before a 2025 move to Real Madrid, Partizan and Anadolu Efes. Mixed outcome: a real, multi-team NBA journeyman big for six seasons, never more than deep bench depth.

name: Didi Louzada
notes: A Brazilian wing (Franca club) ranked 61st in the class by ESPN, a mid-round athletic prospect from the Nike Hoop Summit's World Select Team. Atlanta took him 35th (traded to New Orleans). A 25-game suspension for violating the NBA's anti-drug policy and a torn meniscus requiring surgery combined to wreck his development — just 12 total NBA games (3.6 ppg) across three seasons before Portland waived him in 2022, ending his NBA run before age 23. Bust: modest draft-slot upside further undercut by suspension and injury.

name: Cody Martin
notes: Nevada's Mountain West Defensive Player of the Year as a junior (14.0/6.3/4.7), a defense-first forward with modest scoring production for the position. Charlotte took him 36th. Martin developed into a real, useful Hornets rotation piece over five seasons (a 7.7 ppg, career-best .482 FG% peak in 2021-22) before a serious quad injury in 2022 limited him going forward, leading to a 2025 trade to Phoenix, a brief Indiana stint, and a 2026 G League assignment. Mixed outcome: a real, multi-year NBA rotation role built on defense, injuries eventually shrinking it.

name: Deividas Sirvydis
notes: A Lithuanian wing who won Adidas Next Generation Tournament MVP as a youth prospect, taken more on projection than a deep scouting record. Dallas took him 37th (traded to Detroit). Sirvydis barely played in the NBA — 23 total games across two seasons (1.9 ppg), repeatedly waived by Detroit and then Indiana — before his career shifted to the G League and, by 2023, back to Europe, where he's become a productive EuroCup scorer. Bust at the NBA level, a real European scorer since.

name: Daniel Gafford
notes: An Arkansas sophomore breakout (16.9/8.6/1.9 blk, First-Team All-SEC and All-Defensive) after a stunning perfect-shooting freshman debut, elite rim-running and rim protection from a non-Power-Five-adjacent conference background. Chicago took him 38th. Gafford developed gradually (a $40.2M Wizards extension, an 84.6% shooting playoff stretch) before a 2024 trade to Dallas fully unlocked him — an NBA-leading 72.5% field goal percentage, a near-record 33 straight made shots, a Finals run, and a $54M extension. Hit: elite college efficiency that became a genuine, highly efficient starting-caliber NBA center.

name: Alen Smailagić
notes: An 18-year-old Serbian big man who became the youngest player ever in G League history, a draft-and-develop project (9.1/4.0 in his G League debut season) rather than a finished prospect. New Orleans took him 39th (traded to Golden State). Smailagić never found real NBA minutes (29 games across two seasons, 3.0 ppg) before Golden State waived him at 20 — but he's since become a genuine winner in Europe, an ABA League champion with Partizan (2023) and an LKL champion with Žalgiris (2025). Bust at the NBA level, a real European title-winner since.

name: Justin James
notes: An unheralded Wyoming recruit (one high-major offer) who became the Mountain West's scoring leader as a senior (22.1/8.5/4.4, third-most points in conference history), real production that NBA evaluators nonetheless left largely unranked. Sacramento took him 40th on the strength of character references alone. James never found an NBA role (72 games, 3.2 ppg) before his career shifted to the G League, Europe and Taiwan. Bust: dominant mid-major production that never crossed over to NBA-level competition.

name: Eric Paschall
notes: A Fordham transfer who broke out as a Villanova senior (16.5/6.2, First-Team All-Big East, a 10-of-11 Final Four outing against Kansas), real interior scoring polish. Golden State took him 41st. Paschall delivered immediately — All-Rookie First Team, 14.0 ppg as a rookie — before a trade to Utah saw his role and production shrink (5.8, then 2.0 ppg), and he was out of the NBA by 2023, his career shifting to Puerto Rico, Italy, China and Japan. Mixed outcome: a genuinely productive rookie season that never sustained beyond Golden State.

name: Admiral Schofield
notes: Tennessee's First-Team All-SEC senior (16.5/6.1, AP Honorable Mention All-American) on a Sweet 16 team, good size (6'6", 240 lb) but modest, still-developing three-point range (41.8% as a senior) the flagged NBA question. Philadelphia took him 42nd (traded to Washington). Schofield never secured real NBA minutes (131 games across five seasons with Orlando and Washington, 3.3 ppg) despite multiple two-way looks. Bust: solid college production and physical tools that never translated into an NBA rotation role.

name: Jaylen Nowell
notes: Washington's Pac-12 Player of the Year as a sophomore, leading the Huskies to a regular-season title, real scoring instincts and competitiveness that carried him to an early declaration. Minnesota took him 43rd. Nowell developed gradually into a real bench scorer (a 10.8 ppg peak in 2022-23, a playoff debut) before his role diminished through Memphis, Detroit and New Orleans stints, his career shifting to China and, by 2026, Turkey's Beşiktaş. Mixed outcome: a real, multi-year NBA scoring role at his Minnesota peak, never sustained beyond it.

name: Bol Bol
notes: A polarizing 7'3" Oregon freshman (21/9.6/2.7 blk on a stunning 56/52% shooting split) whose season ended with a foot injury in December, real lottery-caliber talent undercut by durability concerns that were already the whole story. He fell to 44th (Miami, traded to Denver). Chronic injuries defined the NBA career — marginal Denver minutes (2.4 ppg over three years), a real look in Orlando (a 26-point game), decline in Phoenix — before a brief Philippines comeback (a 53-point game) ended in another season-ending injury by 2026. Bust: the exact durability risk flagged pre-draft is what the whole career became.

name: Isaiah Roby
notes: A Nebraska junior with real shot-blocking and rebounding production (11.8/6.9/1.9 blk, most Nebraska blocks by a sophomore since 2001), athletic tools with a limited offensive repertoire the flag. Detroit took him 45th (traded to Dallas). Roby's best stretch came with Oklahoma City (8.7 ppg in 2020-21, a 30-point game), but he never held a lasting rotation spot — 151 total games across four teams before falling to the G League and overseas by the mid-2020s. Bust: real athletic and defensive tools that never developed a full enough offensive game.

name: Talen Horton-Tucker
notes: A four-star Iowa State freshman (11.8/4.9/2.3/1.3 stl, a 26-point/14-rebound outing against Illinois) who declared after one season, real all-around upside from a thin sample. Orlando took him 46th (traded to the Lakers). Horton-Tucker became the second-youngest champion in NBA history at 19 (2020), developed real scoring flashes (a 40-point game, later a 41-point game with Utah), before a 2022 trade and a 2024-25 Chicago stint led to a move to Turkey's Fenerbahçe in 2025 — where he's since won a EuroLeague Second Team nod and Turkish league titles. Mixed outcome: a real, championship-tenured NBA career with genuine scoring upside, ultimately finding more expanded stardom in Europe.

name: Ignas Brazdeikis
notes: Michigan's Big Ten Freshman of the Year (14.8 ppg on 46.2/39.2% shooting, Second-Team All-Big Ten), a prolific scorer whose modest assist rate (0.8) and limited floor game raised real NBA-wing-versatility questions. Sacramento took him 47th (traded to New York). Brazdeikis never found consistent NBA minutes (a scattered 1.9-11.1 ppg across Knicks, 76ers and Magic stints, never more than 42 games in a season) before shifting to Europe by 2022. Bust: elite college scoring efficiency that never resolved the flagged versatility concerns.

name: Terance Mann
notes: Florida State's all-around senior (11.4/6.5, one of only three Seminoles ever with 1,200 points/600 rebounds/200 assists/100 steals), a well-rounded role player rather than a projected scorer or creator. LA Clippers took him 48th. Mann developed patiently (2.4 to 10.8 ppg over three seasons) into a real winning-team contributor — a signature 39-point, Game 6 comeback performance in the 2021 Conference Semifinals that sent the Clippers to their first Conference Finals — a $47M extension in 2024, then trades to Atlanta and Brooklyn by 2025-26. Hit: a role player whose patient development produced a genuine, franchise-relevant NBA career.

name: Quinndary Weatherspoon
notes: Mississippi State's two-time Howell Trophy winner (Mississippi's top player) and First-Team All-SEC senior, the program's third 2,000-point scorer, solid four-year production without a standout translatable NBA skill. San Antonio took him 49th. Weatherspoon spent his first two seasons mostly on Austin's G League two-way roster before signing with Golden State in 2021 and winning a championship ring in 2022, though his career minutes stayed marginal throughout before shifting to China, Puerto Rico, Russia and Canada. Bust as a rotation player, though a real championship-roster NBA experience.

name: Jarrell Brantley
notes: College of Charleston's do-it-all senior (19.0/8.4, First Team All-CAA, third-most points in program history), real production from a mid-major without elite measurables. Indiana took him 50th (traded to Utah). Brantley's NBA run stayed marginal (41 games across three seasons with the Jazz, 2.7 ppg) before a 2021 waiver sent his career to Russia, the G League, Puerto Rico and New Zealand (a Club MVP award), with a brief 2023 Jazz 10-day contract before settling in Japan. Bust: solid mid-major production that never crossed into a real NBA role.

name: Tremont Waters
notes: LSU's elite freshman floor general (15.9/6.0/3.4, breaking Ben Simmons's school freshman assist record) who developed into an All-SEC First Teamer, real playmaking undercut by a 5'10" frame. Boston took him 51st. Waters was G League Rookie of the Year but never crossed over — 40 total NBA games across Boston, Toronto and Washington (3.7/2.1) — the gap between G League dominance and NBA-level physicality proving decisive. Bust: elite lead-guard production that never survived NBA size and speed.

name: Jalen McDaniels
notes: San Diego State's productive sophomore (15.9/8.3, four-star pedigree, a Combine invite), real two-way tools for a long forward. Charlotte took him 52nd. McDaniels developed into a genuine four-year Hornets rotation piece (a 10.6 ppg peak in 2022-23) before trades to Philadelphia, Toronto (a disappointing 3.4 ppg) and Sacramento saw his role shrink, ending with a 2025 Washington 10-day deal and a 2026 move to Japan. Mixed outcome: several real years of NBA rotation value, never sustained beyond Charlotte.

name: Justin Wright-Foreman
notes: Hofstra's back-to-back CAA Player of the Year, a national top-5 scorer as a junior (24.2 ppg) capped by a 48-point, school-record-tying senior outburst — elite mid-major scoring volume. Utah took him 53rd. Wright-Foreman's NBA chance was brief (4 two-way games, 4.8 ppg) before his career shifted to a genuinely successful international run — CEBL scoring titles in 2023 and 2024 — now playing in Spain's Liga ACB. Bust at the NBA level, a real professional scorer elsewhere.

name: Marial Shayok
notes: A redshirt senior scoring breakout at Iowa State (18.7 ppg, 2nd in the Big 12, Big 12 Tournament MVP on 49.6/38.6/87.8% shooting), efficient, well-rounded production. Philadelphia took him 54th. Shayok's NBA look was brief (4 two-way games, 2.8 ppg) before a long, genuinely successful international career — Turkey, China, Israel's Maccabi Tel Aviv, and by 2026 Montenegro — plus representing South Sudan at the 2023 World Cup and 2024 Olympics. Bust at the NBA level, a real international pro and national team player since.

name: Kyle Guy
notes: Virginia's 2019 NCAA Tournament Most Outstanding Player and national champion, an elite college shooter (17.4 ppg senior year, a 49.5% three-point freshman season) whose modest size (6'1") and limited playmaking were the flagged NBA translation risks. Sacramento took him 55th (traded to Miami). Guy's NBA career never got going — 53 games across three seasons (3.1 ppg on 30.3% from three, a dramatic efficiency collapse) before falling out of the league by 2022. Bust: a tournament legend whose shooting never once translated to NBA-level defenses.

name: Jaylen Hands
notes: A five-star UCLA point guard recruit (No. 3 nationally) who led the Pac-12 in assists as a sophomore (6.1), real playmaking pedigree. LA Clippers took him 56th (traded to Brooklyn). Hands never signed an NBA contract, going straight to the G League (11.3/3.5 with Long Island) before his rights moved to Detroit and were renounced — his career shifting fully to Europe, where he's become a genuine star, the 2025 Lega Basket Serie A scoring leader with Varese. Never played in the NBA — a real, decorated European scoring guard instead.

name: Jordan Bone
notes: A modestly-recruited Tennessee guard (247Sports' 171st-ranked recruit) who broke out as a junior (13.5/5.8/3.2, Second-Team All-SEC), real late-blooming production. New Orleans took him 57th (traded to Detroit). Bone's NBA chance was brief (24 games across two teams, 2.8 ppg) before his career shifted to Turkey, Spain and Italy, most recently HLA Alicante in 2026. Bust: a real college breakout that only got a token NBA look.

name: Miye Oni
notes: Yale's Ivy League Player of the Year (a 35-point game against Princeton, Coach K predicting a first-round selection), the first Ivy Leaguer drafted since 1995 — real scoring and physical tools from a non-power-conference background. Golden State took him 58th (traded to Utah). Oni never secured lasting NBA minutes (3.5, then 1.9 ppg across two seasons) before a quick Oklahoma City waiver and a brief New Orleans 10-day deal ended the chance, his career shifting to London, Spain and Puerto Rico. Bust: an Ivy League star whose college dominance never crossed over to NBA-level competition.

name: Dewan Hernandez
notes: A five-star Miami recruit (11.4/6.6 on 57% FG as a sophomore) whose junior season was wiped out by NCAA corruption-scandal eligibility issues, real physical tools with a thin, disrupted college sample. Toronto took him 59th. Hernandez's NBA chance was brief (6 games, 2.3 ppg) but included a genuine bubble-season clutch moment against Philadelphia, before a 2020 waiver sent his career through the G League, Israel, Greece, China and, by 2026, Korea's KBL. Bust: real recruiting pedigree that scandal-disrupted college development and thin NBA opportunity never let show up.

name: Vanja Marinković
notes: A Serbian wing (Partizan Belgrade's youth system) taken with the very last pick of the 2019 draft — the 60th selection — a pure long-shot flier with minimal detailed scouting record. Sacramento took him, his rights traded four more times (Clippers, Grizzlies, Nets, back to the Clippers) without ever converting. Marinković never played in the NBA, instead building a genuinely solid European career through Valencia and Saski Baskonia in Spain before returning to Partizan as team captain in 2024. Never played in the NBA — Mr. Irrelevant of 2019 became a real European club captain instead.
